data.turoyo: W du šrolo ftiḥo ste ṭalabe lə ṭləble. ʕAm hawxa dayəm mankarre u gəšmayḏe u əmṯonoyo w u knəšyoyo. W lo bas hawxa, kul naqqa dəšše w mdašdašše bayn dar raġloṯo. <...>
data.translation: And in truth, it did not even make its demands openly. Yet it always denied its national and social being. And not only that: every time it trampled and crushed it underfoot. <...>

rationale: Thin I.1 Preterit cell; underfoot phrase and coordinated trampling provide evidence of a social participant extension. Exact referents remain unresolved. English is supplied project machine translation.

summary: Jan Beṯ-Şawoce has no edition translation. English accompanying the added examples is the supplied project machine translation, copied and cut without retranslation; lexical decisions rest on the Turoyo.

The existing example has a reciprocal crowd. Jan instead coordinates dəšše with mdašdašše and specifies bayn dar raġloṯo; this shifts participant configuration without proving a new stem or Detransitive.
The inherited I label for the reduplicated root is retained. No etymology or source spelling is changed.
Repetition kul naqqa gives a recurrent discourse frame around a Preterit form; it does not turn that form into Infectum.
Jan 3.10/111: identify the subject of mankarre/dəšše/mdašdašše and the referent of u gəšmayḏe. Does underfoot denote literal violence or a conventional expression of social oppression?

The context of national and social being gives trampling underfoot a likely social oppression application. The actor and affected referent remain implicit, and no narrower humiliation sense is asserted.
